newsitem.title: UK: Pru denies dragging feet in pensions review.
newsitem.headline: Pru denies dragging feet in pensions review.

text.p: British insurer Prudential Corporation Plc on Wednesday denied accusations it was dragging its feet over an investigation into pensions mis-selling.
"We do not accept the accusation that we are dragging our feet," a Prudential spokesman told Reuters.

Earlier the daily Independent newspaper said that Prudential, the UK's biggest personal pensions provider, topped a regulator's list of the worst offenders in a scandal where hundreds of thousands of people may have been wrongly advised to transfer to a personal pension.

The paper said it had obtained a Personal Investment Authority (PIA) document, which showed that only 14,000 policyholders out of 560,000 cases under review in the UK had been offered compensation totalling 26.75 million stg. The paper said Prudential had completed only 10 assessments of over 41,000 priority pension review cases.
The spokesman declined to comment on the figures, but stressed the company was working hard at completing the review.
He said the number of priority cases was not an indication of how many could have been poorly advised to transfer to personal pension plans.

Many of the companies participating in the review have missed target dates, by which they were due to complete the investigation of most of the cases. They were due to finish a first tranche of review cases by the end of last year. However, several of those firms concerned have already said that they have encountered difficulties in obtaining information from occupational pension schemes and individuals, whose input is needed.

The Prudential has sent out over 660,000 questionnaires. The PIA declined to comment on the Independent report, but is due within the next two to three weeks to publish a statistical update on the progress of the pensions review.

In April the PIA said around 1.1 million cases had been identified, of which 390,000 were considered a priority. At that time, redress had been offered in 7,000 cases and 6.6 million stg in compensation paid.

Britain's largest trade union UNISON said the figures printed in the Independent vindicated its decision to take legal action against companies which have failed to offer its members compensation. Self regulation did not work, it added.
"The agony of uncertainty experienced by thousands of people who feel their financial security is at risk is quite unacceptale," press officer Glyn Jenkins said in a statement.
